main_message: Gibraltar was fought over for centuries because of its position and its sea, and the quarrel has moved from sieges to runways, fences and border paperwork, told with both sides' sources.

claims_doubted.quote: Historians on both sides count fourteen sieges of it, between 1309 and 1783.
claims_doubted.why: Spanish and British historians do not agree on one fixed count; it depends on what you call a siege (Sayer, García Sanz and the museum each count differently). 'Both sides count fourteen' is too neat and the title leans on it.

claims_doubted.quote: Its commanders, Admiral George Rooke and Prince George of Hesse-Darmstadt, came in the name of "Charles the Third."
claims_doubted.why: True as far as it goes, but Rooke's fleet took the Rock for the Archduke and then raised the English flag, not Charles's. The video never says that, and that act is the root of the Spanish grievance.

claims_doubted.quote: Townspeople could stay if they swore loyalty to "Charles the Third." Almost all of them left.
claims_doubted.why: Presented as a choice. In Spanish accounts the departure was near-total and the terms were not honoured in practice, with the Gibraltarian refugees (the 'Ciudad de Gibraltar en San Roque') as a founding grievance. 'Almost all' with no source on who counted is soft.

claims_doubted.quote: Spain tried to take Gibraltar back from 1704 to 1705, with French troops, and again in 1727. Neither siege took it.
claims_doubted.why: Omits that the 1704-05 siege came close, and glosses the 1713 Treaty's other clauses; also says nothing of the sieges in between that the 'fourteen' count would include. The sequence is thin.

claims_doubted.quote: The treaty never mentions the sandy isthmus to the north. Spain says the isthmus was never ceded. Britain says Gibraltar includes it.
claims_doubted.why: Britain's position is mostly based on possession and prescription (long occupation), not on the treaty text. Stated as two equal assertions, it hides that the treaty text favours Spain here.

claims_doubted.quote: Scurvy spread, until a Danish ship full of lemons was brought in.
claims_doubted.why: Told as a neat anecdote; the lemon-ship story is from British narratives and the timeline is unclear. No source on screen.

claims_doubted.quote: Four days later, the French and Spanish fleets sailed in, under the Duc de Crillon
claims_doubted.why: Crillon commanded the land forces and overall assault, but the fleet was under Admiral Córdoba, and the combined fleets were not 'sailing in' on that date in the way suggested. Command is muddled.

claims_doubted.quote: By September 1782, about seven and a half thousand men held the Rock.
claims_doubted.why: No counter named. It is also placed oddly after the half-million rounds line, with no sense of how many Spanish and French besiegers there were at that point (the 14,000 figure is from 1779).

claims_doubted.quote: Between them, the two sides fired nearly half a million rounds.
claims_doubted.why: Unsourced total, and 'rounds' is vague. Who tallied it?

claims_doubted.quote: The Rock was never starved out.
claims_doubted.why: Reasonable, but it skips that the blockade was repeatedly broken by relief fleets and the Spanish naval blockade was porous. The sentence reads as British resilience rather than a failure of the blockade.

claims_doubted.quote: Today, the tunnels add up to about fifty-five kilometres, more than the roads above ground.
claims_doubted.why: A figure that circulates widely, but usually quoted as 'about 34 miles' by British sources. The comparison with the surface roads is checkable and unsourced.

claims_doubted.quote: On the night of the seventh of November 1942, at least six hundred and fifty aircraft lined the runway.
claims_doubted.why: Plausible for Operation Torch staging, but no source, and 'at least' is a hedge on a number I would want attributed.

claims_doubted.quote: In July 2026, Britain and the EU signed a treaty to take the checks off this border.
claims_doubted.why: Very recent event stated flatly; the next lines correct it to 'provisional'. A viewer hearing it once would take 'signed' as final.

claims_doubted.quote: In October 2025, people living in Spain held more than four in ten of Gibraltar's jobs.
claims_doubted.why: Source not named in narration. And 'four in ten', 'fifteen thousand' and 'fourteen thousand' are three different framings of the same group that do not obviously agree.

one_sided.quote: Prince George of Hesse-Darmstadt, came in the name of "Charles the Third."
one_sided.why: Frames the capture as a dynastic-war act on behalf of a Habsburg claimant. It never says the Rock was then held by Britain for itself, which is how Spain tells it: a seizure.

one_sided.quote: the Treaty of Utrecht made it permanent: the town, castle and port went to the British Crown, "for ever."
one_sided.why: Quotes 'for ever' but the reversion clause (it must return to Spain if Britain ever gives it up) comes only in a clipped way, and Spain's view that Utrecht was imposed after the war is absent.
Framed as British success; says nothing of the fact that these were Spanish and French attempts to recover their own territory, which is the Spanish framing.

one_sided.quote: Its boats at Algeciras had one job: to cut off the food reaching the Rock from Africa.
one_sided.why: Casts Algeciras as a starving machine. In Spanish telling it was a standard naval blockade of an enemy fortress in wartime, and the town (my town) is reduced to a hunger tool.

one_sided.quote: By January 1780, thistles, dandelions and wild leeks were daily food for many; an egg cost sixpence.
one_sided.why: Strong British suffering detail from garrison memoirs, with no comparable Spanish or French hardship shown (the besiegers' camp sickness, supply failures).

one_sided.quote: Two days later, soldiers broke into the merchants' stores. A British officer blamed "resentment and intoxication."
one_sided.why: Quotes the officer's excuse without saying whether anyone else disagreed; it softens looting by the garrison.

one_sided.quote: The garrison's answer was heat: cannonballs heated red-hot, so that whatever they hit caught fire.
one_sided.why: Heroic framing of the garrison's cleverness. The attackers get the clumsy-design side: 'It was refused' about the test.
Sixteen dead against more than two thousand attackers is the headline, and it is the garrison's own count. Fair to label it, but the contrast is allowed to stand alone.

one_sided.quote: More than two thousand attackers were lost, by British and Spanish counts
one_sided.why: Actually a rare fair line, but 'attackers lost' blurs killed, drowned, wounded and captured, which makes it look worse for Spain than the on-screen detail does.

one_sided.quote: With Spain's consent, the British blew up the Spanish forts.
one_sided.why: Leans on consent as the whole story. Spanish scholars stress the occupation of the neutral ground afterwards was by creep, and the screen then softens it with 'Montero gives 1811'.

one_sided.quote: The fence went up in 1909; Spain has never recognised it as a border.
one_sided.why: Fair, but the 'act of courtesy' quote is used as Britain's own admission without the British answer.

one_sided.quote: For the rest of the war, a Spanish scholar found, Spain protested British ships in its waters, but not the airstrip.
one_sided.why: Spain under Franco was not a free actor in 1940-45. Leaving out why it stayed quiet makes this read as acceptance.

one_sided.quote: Those tunnels became a city inside the Rock
one_sided.why: Admiring, romantic wording. Nothing similar is said for the Spanish side's works.

one_sided.quote: Our read: the rich-looking number partly rests on the other side.
one_sided.why: The narrator drops into editorial voice. The arithmetic caveat is good but 'rests on the other side' is an opinion, said right after the video promised a balanced telling.

one_sided.quote: In June 1969, Spain closed the land frontier completely.
one_sided.why: Gives only the Spanish act. Omits the Gibraltar constitution of 1969 and the Franco-era context of the 1967 referendum, so the closure reads as arbitrary.

casualty_counter_missing.why: Not a casualty but a population figure with no counter. Who counted the departures from 1704?

casualty_counter_missing.quote: Governor Diego de Salinas had barely a hundred soldiers, by a Spanish count.
casualty_counter_missing.why: Good: the counter is named, and then British 'up to five hundred' is balanced. But the 'fifteen thousand rounds' that follows has no counter at all.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: More than two thousand attackers were lost, by British and Spanish counts; three hundred and fifty-seven were rescued.
casualty_counter_missing.why: Two sides named, but the on-screen split (185 hit by gunfire, 357 rescued) is attributed to a French account and a British return, and the narration does not say so. Heard once, the viewer gets none of those labels.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: From all causes, Montero put the losses near two thousand inside and six thousand outside.
casualty_counter_missing.why: Montero (1860) is a Spanish historian writing 77 years later, with no stated source for his figures. The narration then sets 'at least eight hundred and seventy dead' against it, which is not the same thing as two thousand, so the viewer can't compare.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: The garrison's own records count at least eight hundred and seventy dead.
casualty_counter_missing.why: The counter is named (garrison's own), but the figure leaves out scurvy deaths in 1779-80, which the on-screen card admits and the voice does not.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: Between them, the two sides fired nearly half a million rounds.
Some four thousand six hundred Spanish day workers were cut off.
casualty_counter_missing.why: No source given for the workers figure, and it is a Spanish-side number.

hard_to_follow.quote: Since July 2026, this gate has had no routine checks.
hard_to_follow.why: Opens with a claim that is contradicted at the end ('provisional', 'fence a few metres behind'). A viewer hearing it once will be confused about whether the border is open.

hard_to_follow.quote: So why, today, is the fight over it about paperwork and payrolls?
hard_to_follow.why: 'Payrolls' is not explained anywhere before the last chapter. The hook promises something the middle does not deliver for eight minutes.

hard_to_follow.quote: On the fourth of August 1704, Gibraltar surrendered. English histories say the twenty-fourth of July, on the old calendar.
hard_to_follow.why: Two dates and a calendar change in one breath. Heard once, it sounds like a contradiction.

hard_to_follow.quote: Austria, England and the Dutch backed a rival for Spain's crown; France backed Madrid's king.
hard_to_follow.why: A whole War of the Spanish Succession in one sentence, with no names. Hard to hold when heard once.

hard_to_follow.quote: forty-seven ships of the line by the British count, fifty by the Spanish.
hard_to_follow.why: Numbers in quick succession; the point (two counts) is lost unless you see the screen.

hard_to_follow.quote: At half past nine, the batteries moved into position. At a quarter to ten, the garrison opened fire. At ten twenty-five, by the Spanish account, some four hundred guns answered together.
hard_to_follow.why: Four clock times in three sentences. Nobody holds that by ear. Also 'four hundred guns answered together': answered whom?

hard_to_follow.quote: By early July, Sergeant Ince's thirteen men had cut about eighty-two feet of solid rock.
hard_to_follow.why: Sudden digression into tunnelling, in the middle of the September 1782 battle story. A viewer loses the thread and the chronology.

hard_to_follow.quote: Remember this street. We'll come back to it.
hard_to_follow.why: Good device, but the street is never named, so on audio alone there is nothing to remember.

hard_to_follow.quote: Subscribe if you'd like the next place in this series.
hard_to_follow.why: Dropped into the middle of the film, between the 1934 airstrip and the 1939 runway. Breaks the flow.

hard_to_follow.quote: That divides by the thirty-eight thousand who live there, and leaves out the people in Spain who hold fourteen thousand of its jobs.
hard_to_follow.why: 'Divides by' is the wrong verb for a per-capita figure and the sentence hangs on three numbers spoken fast. Needs to be simplified or shown only.

hard_to_follow.quote: The old fence is coming down, but a new one stands a few metres behind it, with about a hundred and fifty metres left open.
hard_to_follow.why: Hard to picture by ear; what is the 150 metres?

boring_or_slow.from_quote: Spain tried to take Gibraltar back from 1704 to 1705, with French troops, and again in 1727.
boring_or_slow.why: A flat run of dates and treaty clauses with no human story. This is where I would drift.

boring_or_slow.from_quote: The thirteenth of September 1782. At half past nine, the batteries moved into position.
boring_or_slow.why: The big battle is told as a timetable. The most dramatic day of the film is delivered with the least drama.

boring_or_slow.from_quote: All that summer, the garrison had also been digging through the north face.
boring_or_slow.why: Engineering detail that stalls the story just after the climax.

boring_or_slow.from_quote: After that, the edge kept moving.
boring_or_slow.why: Abstract talk of an edge moving, a fence, courtesy. A long stretch with only silent maps and no person or event.

boring_or_slow.from_quote: Then Britain pushed it out into the bay, with stone blasted from the north face and rubble from new tunnels.
boring_or_slow.why: Run of construction facts and statistics; the silent shot afterwards adds length without information.

boring_or_slow.why: Economics by ear with a stack of figures. The thesis of the film's ending is carried by the dullest passage.

top3_fixes: Replace the 'fourteen sieges' claim with the honest line that counts differ (name the three sources and what each counts), and either list the fourteen briefly on screen or drop the number from the title. Right now the whole film is sold on a count it never itemises.

Fix the casualty passages for ear, not eye: say aloud who counted each figure ('the garrison's own return says sixteen dead; the French inquiry says one hundred eighty-five attackers were shot before the fires...'), and cut the Montero losses and the 870 figure down to one comparable pair, flagging that scurvy deaths are missing. Also cut the 13 September timetable to two clock times.

Rebalance and re-pace: add the Spanish framing of 1704 (the raising of the English flag, the exile to San Roque, Utrecht's reversion clause, the Franco-era limits on Spain's wartime protests), drop the editorial 'Our read', move 'Subscribe' to the end, and name the 'street' you ask viewers to remember. Replace the opening 'no routine checks' claim with the provisional status so the first line and the last agree.
_prompt:
You are a Spanish history teacher from Algeciras who reads English well. You know the Gibraltar story from Spanish sources and you notice when an English-language video tilts toward the British side, uses loaded words, or counts casualties without saying who counted.

Below is the complete narration script of a documentary YouTube video titled "Why Gibraltar Was Besieged 14 Times" (about 11 minutes, English narration, animated maps and 3D reconstructions). Lines in [On screen: ...] are text shown on screen at that moment; [silent shot] means picture and music only. Read all of it as yourself and answer honestly. Do not be polite; you have no stake in who made it.

Check especially: (a) factual claims that seem wrong, overstated or missing a source; (b) sentences that favour one side (British or Spanish) by wording, emphasis or omission; (c) any casualty or loss number that does not say who counted it; (d) sentences that are hard to understand when heard once; (e) stretches where you would get bored or leave.

Return ONLY this JSON (no other text). In every "quote", copy the exact words from the script (a short exact phrase is fine):

 "would_keep_watching_after_30s": true|false, "hook_1to10": n, "trust_1to10": n, "balance_1to10": n, "overall_1to10": n,

 "casualty_counter_missing": [{"chapter": "...", "quote": "...", "why": "..."}],

=== SCRIPT ===
## Midnight at the Gate
Midnight at the Gibraltar frontier. To walk in from Spain, you cross an airport runway.
Since July 2026, this gate has had no routine checks.
The Rock sits at the western gate of the Mediterranean.
Historians on both sides count fourteen sieges of it, between 1309 and 1783.
This is why everyone fought over it, told from both sides' records.
[On screen: "A history explainer · every date sourced · British and Spanish records side by side · Facts as of 18 Oct 2026"]
[On screen: number card "14 sieges · 1309–1783" — "Sayer 1862 · García Sanz 2022 · Gibraltar National Museum"]
In 1782, ten floating batteries came to break it.
In 1941, a runway was laid across the only road to Spain.
So why, today, is the fight over it about paperwork and payrolls?

## 1704: A Rock Changes Hands
Austria, England and the Dutch backed a rival for Spain's crown; France backed Madrid's king.
That summer, their fleet sailed into the Bay of Gibraltar.
Its commanders, Admiral George Rooke and Prince George of Hesse-Darmstadt, came in the name of "Charles the Third."
This plan, printed in 1705, shows the prize: a walled town that historians on both sides would call the key of the Mediterranean.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «la preciosa llave del Mediterráneo» — "the precious key of the Mediterranean" · Sayer, 1862: "the key of the Mediterranean"]
Inside, Governor Diego de Salinas had barely a hundred soldiers, by a Spanish count. He refused to surrender. The fleet answered with some fifteen thousand rounds.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «con cien hombres de guarnición … no había artilleros que las sirvieran» — "a garrison of a hundred men … there were no gunners to serve them"]
On the fourth of August 1704, Gibraltar surrendered. English histories say the twenty-fourth of July, on the old calendar.
British accounts put the defenders at up to five hundred, counting armed townsmen.
Townspeople could stay if they swore loyalty to "Charles the Third." Almost all of them left. By Spanish accounts, most settled a league to the north-east, at San Roque.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «se habia acampado en las haciendas cercanas á la ermita de San Roque» — "had camped on the farms near the hermitage of San Roque"]
In 1713, the Treaty of Utrecht made it permanent: the town, castle and port went to the British Crown, "for ever." But "without any territorial jurisdiction, and without any open communication by land."
The treaty never mentions the sandy isthmus to the north. Spain says the isthmus was never ceded. Britain says Gibraltar includes it.
Spain tried to take Gibraltar back from 1704 to 1705, with French troops, and again in 1727. Neither siege took it.
So in 1730, Philip the Fifth ordered a stone line across the isthmus, out of gun range, to cut Gibraltar off by land. The town behind it is still called La Línea: "the line."
[On screen: Gómez Nadal (Almoraima), on Philip V's order of 8 Oct 1730: «bloquear definitivamente la correspondencia y paso a la plaza por tierra» — "to block, once and for all, all contact with and passage to the town by land"]

## The Great Siege
Half a century later came a different question: can you starve a rock? On the twenty-first of June 1779, Madrid closed every link with Gibraltar.
Spain had joined France in its war with Britain. By autumn, about fourteen thousand men faced the Rock across the isthmus.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «Carlos III declaró la guerra á Inglaterra y se unió á Francia» — "Charles III declared war on England and joined France"]
At sea, from mid-July, a Spanish squadron sealed the port. Its boats at Algeciras had one job: to cut off the food reaching the Rock from Africa.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «encaminado principalmente á privar a la plaza de los viveres que le llegaban de las costas de África» — "aimed above all at depriving the town of the food that reached it from the coasts of Africa"]
By January 1780, thistles, dandelions and wild leeks were daily food for many; an egg cost sixpence.
The governor, General Eliott, could hold the walls. The food had to come by sea.
To break the blockade, Britain sent three relief fleets: 1780, 1781, 1782.
Scurvy spread, until a Danish ship full of lemons was brought in.
On the twelfth of April 1781, the second relief convoy dropped anchor, and Spain's batteries opened fire on the town. The townspeople fled south.
Two days later, soldiers broke into the merchants' stores. A British officer blamed "resentment and intoxication."
Between them, the two sides fired nearly half a million rounds.
By September 1782, about seven and a half thousand men held the Rock.
The garrison's answer was heat: cannonballs heated red-hot, so that whatever they hit caught fire. On the eighth of September, they used them in earnest against the Spanish works.
Four days later, the French and Spanish fleets sailed in, under the Duc de Crillon: forty-seven ships of the line by the British count, fifty by the Spanish.
[On screen: Fernández Duro, Armada española (1901): «alegrando la vista los 50 navios que se juntaron en Algeciras» — "the 50 ships of the line that gathered at Algeciras, a joy to see"]
Their answer to red-hot shot: ten floating batteries, designed by the French engineer d'Arçon. A French account says he'd asked to test them against red-hot shot first. It was refused.
[On screen: Conseil de guerre privé (1785): «l'expérience que l'inventeur avoit demandée … à l'épreuve des boulets rouges» — "the test the inventor had asked for … against red-hot shot"]
The thirteenth of September 1782. At half past nine, the batteries moved into position. At a quarter to ten, the garrison opened fire. At ten twenty-five, by the Spanish account, some four hundred guns answered together. By the next morning, all ten batteries were gone.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «á las diez y veinte y cinco minutos de la mañana … rompieron á un tiempo el fuego» — "at twenty-five past ten in the morning … opened fire all at once"]
More than two thousand attackers were lost, by British and Spanish counts; three hundred and fifty-seven were rescued.
[On screen: number card: "> 2,000 lost, prisoners included — British estimate & Montero (Spain)" · "185 hit by gunfire before the fires — French account, 1785" · "357 rescued — British return" · "Garrison: 16 killed — its own return" {S069} {S070} {S071}]
All that summer, the garrison had also been digging through the north face. By early July, Sergeant Ince's thirteen men had cut about eighty-two feet of solid rock.
In July they blasted a hole for air. A Spanish historian wrote it was big enough for a cannon.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «se formó un boquete tan grande … que pareció bien colocar en el un cañón» — "an opening was made so large … that it seemed right to place a cannon in it"]
The Rock was never starved out. In February 1783, word came of a preliminary peace, and on the fifth, the last shot was fired.
From all causes, Montero put the losses near two thousand inside and six thousand outside. The garrison's own records count at least eight hundred and seventy dead. Gibraltar stayed British.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «Los últimos sufrieron una pérdida de cerca de dos mil hombres. La nuestra se aproximó á seis mil por todas causas» — "The latter [the besieged] suffered a loss of nearly two thousand men. Ours came close to six thousand, from all causes" · number card: "Garrison return (Drinkwater): 333 killed or died of wounds · 536 died of sickness (scurvy deaths 1779–80 not included)"]

## The Neutral Ground
Which leaves a question the treaty never answered: where does the Rock end? Between the walls and the Spanish line lay a strip of sand: the neutral ground.
In 1810, with Napoleon's armies heading for the Strait, Spain and Britain were allies. With Spain's consent, the British blew up the Spanish forts.
[On screen: Gómez de Avellaneda: «con autorización española, fueran destruidos por los ingleses» — "with Spanish authorisation, they were destroyed by the British" · "Montero gives 1811"]
After that, the edge kept moving. A Spanish historian describes Britain advancing into the neutral zone step by step.
[On screen: García Sanz, 2022: «el progresivo avance de la frontera sobre la zona neutral» — "the gradual advance of the frontier over the neutral zone"]
On the Spanish side, a town grew up behind the old line. In 1870, it became La Línea de la Concepción.
Remember this street. We'll come back to it.
This was the gap between them: open sand, between two towns.
In 1908, Britain told Spain, "as an act of courtesy," that it would fence the edge of the neutral ground. The fence went up in 1909; Spain has never recognised it as a border.
[On screen: García Sanz, 2022: «"como acto de cortesía"» — "as an act of courtesy"]
Behind the fence: a garrison camp, gardens, rifle ranges, a racecourse.
And in 1934, part of the old racecourse became a grass airstrip. Subscribe if you'd like the next place in this series.

## A Runway on the Isthmus
Why build an airfield on disputed ground? In March 1939, Spain protested that the works stood on "a usurped portion" of its territory.
That November, Spain's foreign minister called the strip a fait accompli, like the Rock itself. Late in 1939, Britain began a hard runway; in 1941, it was laid across the only road to Spain.
[On screen: Spanish government to its London ambassador, 4 Mar 1939 (Marquina Barrio, 1981): «una porción usurpada del territorio nacional» — "a usurped portion of the national territory"]
Then Britain pushed it out into the bay, with stone blasted from the north face and rubble from new tunnels.
Those tunnels became a city inside the Rock: a road about a mile long, a hospital, a power station, dug by British and Canadian tunnellers.
Today, the tunnels add up to about fifty-five kilometres, more than the roads above ground.
This 1943 US Army map shows the town house by house, and the runway reaching into the bay.
June 1940: Spain turns "non-belligerent" and occupies Tangier. Gibraltar sends its women and children away. By 1942, the invasion of North Africa is run from inside the Rock.
[silent shot]
For the rest of the war, a Spanish scholar found, Spain protested British ships in its waters, but not the airstrip.
[On screen: Marquina Barrio, 1981: «no queda constancia de reclamaciones por el uso de la pista» — "there is no record of complaints over the use of the strip"]
On the night of the seventh of November 1942, at least six hundred and fifty aircraft lined the runway. The invasion fleets, from Britain and the United States, came through the Strait.

## The Gate
After the war, the argument returned to the gate. In June 1969, Spain closed the land frontier completely.
Some four thousand six hundred Spanish day workers were cut off. The gate fully reopened in 1985.
The same square, today. In October 2025, people living in Spain held more than four in ten of Gibraltar's jobs.
The UK government puts the daily crossers at about fifteen thousand. People on foot still cross the runway.
And on the other side of the gate.
Remember this street? In 2024, La Línea's unemployment was twenty-eight point six percent: the highest of a hundred and thirteen Spanish cities.
Here's the twist. Gibraltar's government puts output per resident at about eighty-five thousand pounds.
That divides by the thirty-eight thousand who live there, and leaves out the people in Spain who hold fourteen thousand of its jobs. Our read: the rich-looking number partly rests on the other side.
In July 2026, Britain and the EU signed a treaty to take the checks off this border.
It says it changes neither side's position on sovereignty. The old fence is coming down, but a new one stands a few metres behind it, with about a hundred and fifty metres left open.
As of 18 October 2026, the treaty is provisional, pending a European Parliament vote indicated for the fourteenth of December.
So why did everyone fight over this place? Where it sits, and the sea that could feed it. A wall in 1704. A line in 1730. A fence in 1909. A runway in 1941.
[silent shot]
In 1730, Spain built a line to cut the Rock off by land. Today, four in ten of the Rock's jobs are held by people who live beyond it. The last siege ended in 1783. The argument didn't. Next in Contested Places: London, 1666.
